propositions.label: Intelligence explosion
propositions.criterion: A machine (or machine-augmented) intelligence, once capable enough, increases intelligence further through its own design or research capacity, giving a runaway or rapidly compounding rise.

unification.note: The same criterion in both packs, apart from their sentences on term-level uses, which the usual name and the earliest-located-term role replace.

packCriteria.antecedents: A machine (or machine-augmented) intelligence, once capable enough, increases intelligence further through its own design or research capacity, giving a runaway or rapidly compounding rise. Term-level uses of "intelligence explosion" are recorded separately.

propositions.label: Seed AI
propositions.criterion: An initial AI deliberately designed as a starting point that will improve its own design or code toward greater intelligence.

unification.note: The same criterion in both packs, apart from the 1996–2022 pack’s sentence on term-level uses, which the usual name and the earliest-located-term role replace.

packCriteria.antecedents: An initial AI deliberately designed as a starting point that will improve its own design or code toward greater intelligence.

propositions.label: Recursive self-improvement
propositions.criterion: A system improves its own capacity to improve itself, so that each improvement feeds the next (self-augmentation, self-enhancement). Learning from experience or teaching alone does not meet the criterion, and neither does building a better successor, or adding machines to a population, unless the same system is improved.

unification.note: The 1996–2022 criterion, with the antecedents pack’s exclusion of learning and teaching; the usual name and the earliest-located-term role replace the sentence on term-level uses. The successor exclusion applies the Claude check’s finding on Good 1965 (fix 2): successor construction is recorded as context with that element named, rather than widening the criterion to successor lineages.

packCriteria.antecedents: A system improves its own capacity to improve itself, so that each improvement feeds the next (self-augmentation, self-enhancement). Learning from experience or teaching alone does not meet this criterion.

propositions.label: Fast or hard takeoff
propositions.criterion: The transition from roughly human-level to far superhuman capability happens over a short period (hours to months), or is named as a “hard” or “fast” takeoff, as opposed to a gradual transition over years or decades. A transition described only as rapid, or rapid relative to biological or historical change, without such a period, does not meet the criterion.

unification.note: The 1996–2022 criterion, with the antecedents pack’s sentence on rapidity without a period, which also matches the GPT check’s ruling on Bostrom 1996-09-04.

packCriteria.candidates: The transition from roughly human-level to far superhuman capability happens over a short period (hours to months), or is named as a "hard" or "fast" takeoff, as opposed to a gradual transition over years or decades.
packCriteria.antecedents: The transition from roughly human-level to far superhuman capability happens over a short period (hours to months), or is named as a "hard" or "fast" takeoff. A transition described only as rapid relative to biological or historical change, without such a period, is context.

propositions.label: AI-automated AI research
propositions.criterion: AI systems carry out the research, design or engineering that advances AI or computing itself, thereby accelerating progress. Machines that only manufacture other machines do not meet the criterion.

unification.note: The 1996–2022 criterion (“AI systems”), with design named explicitly because both packs counted machine design, and the antecedents pack’s manufacture exclusion. The antecedents wording “Machines” is not adopted.

propositions.label: Strategic or race compression
propositions.criterion: Competitive dynamics in which the first developer or first system gains a decisive or self-reinforcing advantage, or in which competition pressures developers to trade safety for speed or for competitive advantage.

unification.note: The 1996–2022 criterion. propositions.criterion: A claim that people may be unable to keep the ability to direct, correct or stop capable machines (the control half), or that a machine may pursue the purpose as specified rather than the purpose intended (the specification half). method: Every role entry in both packs, and every proposition the 1996–2022 pack listed for an item without a role, is classified under the unified criterion.

definitions.earliest-located: The earliest passage meeting the criterion among the texts located by the recorded searches of 1863–2022, dated by when its wording is attested. It is not a claim that no earlier text exists. One per proposition.
definitions.earliest-located-term: The earliest located use of the proposition’s usual name. Recorded separately from the concept: a text can use the name, for example as a title, without meeting the criterion.
definitions.articulation: Meets the criterion; neither earliest located nor most developed.
definitions.most-developed: The fullest treatment among the located texts: the most explicit mechanism, assumptions and argument. An editorial judgement, not a measure. Not assigned where the 1996–2022 search did not look for the proposition.
definitions.contesting: Disputes the proposition, or a premise it depends on.
definitions.context: Bears on the proposition without meeting its criterion; the missing element is named.

dateRule.dated: Each record carries the date the work is dated by: its publication or issue, the Date header of a message, the posting time of a post, or the date the inspected version bears.
dateRule.claimed: A claimed date is an earlier date given for the work that does not date the checked wording, such as a lecture, talk, symposium or draft.
dateRule.attested: An attested date is the later date from which the quoted wording is known, when it survives only in a later version or copy: an archive capture, a reprint marked as changed, a later electronic edition or a relay.
dateRule.earliest: Earliest located is decided by the date of the wording: the attested date where one is recorded, otherwise the record’s own date. A later copy with no dated witness cannot be earliest located.

rules: Roles are assigned per proposition across the combined scope of both packs and this admission (1863–2022), not per pack.

Exactly one articulation per proposition is earliest located; no articulation in the combined scope has wording definitely dated before it. A record whose wording is known only from an undated later copy cannot be earliest located.

A pack headline that the combined scope displaces is kept as a recorded correction with its reasons.

definitions.nonfiction: An essay, paper, letter, lecture, broadcast, message or post in the author’s own voice.
definitions.fiction: A novel or story, or a speech or treatise inside one. The passage records what the work says, not the author’s view.
definitions.satirical: A piece that uses satirical or ironic devices; whether its argument is earnest is uncertain.
definitions.dream: A piece its author frames as a dream.
definitions.relay: The passage reports or summarises another author’s argument without adopting it.

searchNote.scope: The collection records what located texts from 1863 to 2022 say about the propositions below. "Earliest located" means the earliest text found by the searches below. It is not a claim that no earlier text exists.

items: Samuel Butler’s letters in The Press, Christchurch (1863, 1865), read in archived Papers Past pages; the 1863 letter was compared with column images.
Erewhon: the 1872 printing in Internet Archive page images, and the revised text of 1901 in the Project Gutenberg transcription.
Alan Turing’s typescripts in the King’s College archive (1947–1951) and Turing’s 1950 paper in Mind.
Norbert Wiener’s 1960 article in Science and the indexed abstract of Arthur Samuel’s reply.

I. J. Good’s 1965 chapter in two public scans; the Dartmouth proposal (1955), Marvin Minsky (1961), Donald Michie (1968, read in the 1986 reprint) and Ray Solomonoff (1985, read in the author’s later typesetting).
Vernor Vinge’s 1983 Omni column and 1993 NASA proceedings paper; Hans Moravec (1979, 1989); K. Eric Drexler’s Engines of Creation (1986, read in the 1997 web edition) and 1995 forecast.
Usenet: ten bundles of the Carnegie Mellon comp.ai and comp.ai.philosophy archives (3,901 files) and one relayed sci.nanotech post.
The Extropians mailing list from 1996-07-25: all subject lines to 2002-02 screened, and 1,854 matching messages of 1996–2000 searched in full, with 28 more found by following threads.
The SL4 mailing list, 2000–2012: subjects screened in all 142 monthly indexes, and 647 matching messages searched.
Eliezer Yudkowsky’s early web pages, through Internet Archive captures.
Publications of the Singularity Institute and MIRI, mostly in later reprints, with the 2001 web editions compared where they are cited.
The 2008 Hanson–Yudkowsky debate on Overcoming Bias.
LessWrong and the Alignment Forum: selected posts with their first stored versions, and seven topic tags listed by date.
Arbital pages, read through a third-party viewer.
Personal sites of Robin Hanson, Nick Bostrom, Paul Christiano and Bill Hibbard, Ajeya Cotra’s guest post on Cold Takes, and two formally published papers.

methods: Sources were retrieved directly by script, one request at a time, using archive captures where the original page is gone.
Every quotation was compared with the retrieved text, or with page images where a scan has no text layer or its OCR is unreliable.
Internet Archive full-text screens looked for selected wordings before the earliest located texts. Each screen read the first 20 hits and finds only the phrasings searched.

Each record gives the date its work is dated by. Where the quoted wording survives only in a later copy, the record also gives the date from which that wording is attested, and that date decides which text is earliest located.

Two separate machine checks re-examined the candidate records, one by an OpenAI GPT-6 model for 1996–2022 and one by a Claude Opus 5.5 model for the earlier texts. Their corrections are applied. No person has reviewed the records.
gaps: The Extropians list before 1996-07-25, from 1991, is not in the public archive used and was not searched.
HathiTrust full-text search and the Google Books API refused scripted requests on 2026-10-06 (HTTP 403 and 429), so neither library was searched.

Good’s 1965 chapter cites three earlier texts by Good for the explosion argument: a 1951 review of a book by D. R. Hartree, an IBM report of 1959 (RC-115) and "The social implications of artificial intelligence" (The Scientist Speculates, 1962–63). None was retrieved, nor were Good’s talks and drafts of 1962–64.
The search before 1863 used Butler’s own wording, so it could not find earlier statements in other words.
Google Groups refused requests (HTTP 429), and Usenet beyond the ten Carnegie Mellon bundles was not searched.
LessWrong and the Alignment Forum were not searched in full text; comments and linked posts were not read.

Bostrom’s Superintelligence (2014), which later texts credit for the term "treacherous turn", was not read in a legally accessible copy. Christiano’s ai-alignment.com posts (2016–2018) were not searched.
Moravec’s Mind Children (1988) and the 1986 printing of Engines of Creation were not obtained.
Many texts survive only in later versions: reprints marked as changed, archive captures and posts edited after posting. Each record names the version checked.
B6 and C1–C3 were looked for only before mid-1996, so no most-developed text is named for them.
Fiction was not surveyed. Erewhon is the only novel recorded.
searchNote.corrections: A text found later that is earlier than the earliest located text becomes the new earliest located text. The earlier headline stays on record as a correction.

quotations.note: Quotations were matched against the retrieved text after normalising whitespace and typographic marks; "spacing" and "ligature" mark matches that needed whitespace or ligature-tolerant comparison. Quotations from scans with noisy or absent text layers were read on the page images.

quotationLimits.rule: At most 50 words per quotation; at most 400 words per source, or a tenth of a source shorter than 2,000 words; identical passages count once.

retrieval.note: Sequential direct HTTP for this admission, with archive hosts paced at least 9 seconds apart. Sources whose hashes match the candidate packs are noted in their records.

design: A proposition is a concept entity with a `proposition` block: its code, the one criterion texts are classified against, and its usual names.

A record is one claim from a document to a proposition, with one of three predicates: articulates_proposition, contests_proposition or bears_on_proposition. Its evidence is a quotation of at most 50 words where the source permits short quotations, otherwise a labelled paraphrase.
attributes.thought holds the roles, the register, the term of an earliest-located-term record, a qualifier, the missing element of a context record, and claimed and attested dates.

Validation enforces one earliest-located articulation per proposition by wording date, at most one most-developed record, one earliest-located-term record whose evidence uses the name, claimed and attested dates on the right side of the work’s date, and one record per text, proposition and stance.
No relation runs between texts; proposition records are left off the map. Sources gain the kinds book, message and post; a passage quoted for several claims counts once towards its source’s limit.
The release format becomes 1.1: the entity field `proposition` and its CSV columns.
